extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of science, logic, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and conceptual standards for distinguishing genuine induction (generalization from experience) from mere description/colligation, and for assessing the legitimacy and grounds of inductive inferences in scientific reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction (Generalization from Experience)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Induction properly so called... may, then, be summarily defined as Generalization from Experience. It consists in inferring from some individual instances in which a phenomenon is observed to occur, that it occurs in all instances of a certain class; namely, in all which resemble the former, in what are regarded as the material circumstances.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasises that true induction takes observed cases and generalizes to unobserved but similar cases (under specified material circumstances). The challenge is to identify which circumstances are 'material'. Induction is aimed at explanation and prediction (not mere description).

rubrics_metrics.name: Colligation / Description must not be conflated with Induction
rubrics_metrics.description: The operation of summarizing or combining detached observations into a single representation (Colligation of Facts) is a descriptive operation, not an inductive one: e.g., the navigator declaring land to be an island after circumnavigation, or Kepler representing observed planetary places by an ellipse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A colligation describes what has been observed (it may 'sum up' the observations) but does not infer facts beyond what was observed. Anti-pattern: treating a new descriptive conception (ellipse, island) as if it were an inductive inference that adds new knowledge beyond observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction requires inference to unobserved facts and thus a test of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: “Induction is proof; it is inferring something unobserved from something observed: it requires, therefore, an appropriate test of proof; and to provide that test, is the special purpose of inductive logic.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inductive claims must be susceptible to tests that establish the inferred (unobserved) facts. Mere consistency with known observations is insufficient as proof for an inductive claim; inductive logic should supply tests (criteria) for such proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction of a new conception (Invention) is distinct from Induction (Proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mental invention of a new conception (e.g., the idea of an ellipse) is an act of invention or hypothesis-forming, but that invention alone does not constitute induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While new conceptions can be necessary for both description and induction, they are part of invention/design, not the essence of inductive proof. Anti-pattern: following Whewell in equating the presence of a novel conception with having performed an inductive proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colligation is a necessary preparatory step for induction
rubrics_metrics.description: “Without the previous colligation of detached observations by means of one general conception, we could never have obtained any basis for an induction... Induction always presupposes... that the results of these observations are... connected together by general descriptions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good inductive reasoning typically requires first organizing observations into coherent general descriptions (colligations) so that material circumstances and regularities can be identified. Lack of such organization makes induction impracticable for complex phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different descriptive representations can all be correct within limits, but conflicting inductions cannot all be true
rubrics_metrics.description: Different successive general expressions (e.g., circular epicycles, ellipse) may each correctly represent observed facts to the degree of observational precision at the time; however, conflicting explanatory inductions or predictions are not all true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between approximate/descriptive adequacy (multiple representations may serve) and explanatory/predictive truth (only correct inductions survive). Use precision and predictive/explanatory power to adjudicate between competing accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity of nature as the ultimate warrant (major premise) for induction
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposition that the course of nature is uniform (that similar circumstances produce similar results) is the fundamental axiom or ultimate major premise implicit in all inductive inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle is itself an inductive generalization (not an a priori explanation). In syllogistic form, induction often suppresses this major premise; recognising it clarifies that induction rests on an assumed uniformity which must be justified by prior inductive experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of parallel cases and the role of 'material circumstances'
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction presumes 'parallel cases': that what happens once will, under a sufficient degree of similarity of circumstances, happen again; the difficulty lies in specifying which circumstances are material (relevant) and which are not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessing an inductive claim requires careful delineation of the class of cases and the material circumstances that define relevant similarity. Misidentifying material circumstances leads to invalid generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis/Conception selection is tentative and requires skillful guessing plus testing
rubrics_metrics.description: The process of selecting a conception (e.g., Kepler's ellipse) is tentative and consists of successive guesses; successful ones are 'skillful guesses' which must then be tested against observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypothesis formation (invention) is a creative, trial-and-error step; its legitimacy as a basis for description or induction depends on subsequent agreement with observed details. Historical example: Kepler tried many imagined paths before finding the ellipse that matched observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstraction as the descriptive extraction of common characters
rubrics_metrics.description: The mental operation which extracts from a number of detached observations certain general characters in which the observed phenomena resemble one another is Abstraction (used to form descriptions, not necessarily induction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abstraction provides general expressions that connect known facts but by itself does not extend to unknown cases. Use abstraction to form precise descriptive categories before attempting inductive extension.
